# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–23 (Complete – Updated 168)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of sixth year, afternoon/evening of Sunday** (Chapter 23). Rawdon discovered Rebecca with Steyne, confronted them, visited Pitt to arrange guardianship of little Rawdon, and arranged duel with Steyne. Duel now formally initiated; seconds communicating. Amelia continues evening vigils at Russell Square. Little Rawdon at school.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opens "autumn of sixth year." Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton); Queen's Crawley; rural areas including Fenmere, Mirecombe.

## The Catastrophic Discovery and Immediate Aftermath (Chapters 22–23)

**Rawdon's Return Home and Confrontation (Chapter 22–23)**: Found drawing-room blazing with light at nine o'clock. Found Steyne bowing to kiss Rebecca's hand; Rebecca sat in brilliant toilette, arms sparkling with bracelets given by Steyne. Rawdon seized Steyne by neckcloth, struck him twice over face with open hand, flung him bleeding to ground. Steyne wore scar to dying day.

**Jewel and Financial Discovery (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon flung open boxes and wardrobes, found desk containing papers, love-letters, trinkets, and pocket-book. **CRITICAL DISCOVERY**: Bank-notes including fresh note for **one thousand pounds from Lord Steyne**—evidence of extensive financial support constituting payment for sexual favors.

**Rebecca's Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23)**: Remained alone for hours, certain "he would never come back. He was gone forever." Experienced suicidal ideation: considered laudanum. French maid (accomplice, in Steyne's pay) persuaded her to rest. By afternoon, Rebecca awakened when chapel bells rang, rang for maid repeatedly, screamed from landing with hair loose.

**Rebecca's Revelation of Heritage (Chapter 23)**: Rebecca claimed innocence before God. Rawdon screamed: "You're as innocent as your mother, the ballet-girl, and your husband the bully." **REVELATION**: Rebecca's mother was a ballet-girl; her father (characterized by Rawdon) was a bully.

## Rawdon's Actions and Duel Arrangements (Chapter 23)

**Morning Meeting with Pitt (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon arrived at Great Gaunt Street in evening costume worn two days, blood-shot eyed, tumbled clothes. Pitt initially thought Rawdon intoxicated but refused financial help: "Even the hundred pounds that Jane took you last night were promised to my lawyer to-morrow morning."

**Rawdon's Confession and Request (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon spoke in husky voice: "It's the boy. I want you to promise me that you will take charge of him when I'm gone." Revealed full circumstances of financial manipulation and Rebecca's infidelity. Pitt instantly guessed Rawdon intended to duel Steyne. Rawdon asked Pitt to be his friend.

**Financial Settlement (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon drew pocket-book found in Becky's desk: "Here's six hundred--I want you to give the money to Briggs, who lent it to us--and who was kind to the boy--and I've always felt ashamed of having taken the poor old woman's money. And here's some more--I've only kept back a few pounds--which Becky may as well have." Thousand-pound note fell out.

**Challenge to Steyne (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon knocked at Gaunt House, handed card to porter: "Colonel Crawley would be all day after one o'clock at the Regent Club in St. James's Street--not at home." Proceeded to Knightsbridge Barracks.

**Meeting with Captain Macmurdo (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon found Captain Macmurdo at barracks. Macmurdo (age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, best shots and riders in England, Rawdon's former rival, Waterloo veteran). Macmurdo composed letter to Steyne requesting appointment of friend to arrange meeting. Letter delivered to Regent Club.

**Rawdon's Emotional Revelation (Chapter 23)**: Covered face with hands, overcome: "You don't know how fond I was of that one...I followed her like a footman. I gave up everything I had to her. I'm a beggar because I would marry her. By Jove, sir, I've pawned my own watch in order to get her anything she fancied; and she--she's been making a purse for herself all the time, and grudged me a hundred pound to get me out of quod." Showed Macmurdo thousand-pound note as evidence. Gave gold sleeve-buttons as legacy for little Rawdon.

**Preparation for Duel (Chapter 23)**: Macmurdo ordered breakfast with cheerful voice. Both men maintained composure; participated gaily in barracks breakfast conversation as church crowds poured out. Walked to Regent Club on St. James's Street.

## The Dissolution of Curzon Street Household (Chapter 23)

**Mademoiselle Fifine's Abandonment and Theft (Chapter 23)**: Fifine had quit premises on "French leave." After picking up trinkets from drawing-room, packed her own boxes, called cab herself, brought down trunks without aid from other servants, and departed Curzon Street without saying goodbye. "The game, in her opinion, was over in that little domestic establishment."

**Fifine's Thefts**: Secured four richly gilt Louis Quatorze candlesticks, six gilt albums, keepsakes, Books of Beauty, gold enamelled snuff-box once belonging to Madame du Barri, sweetest little inkstand and mother-of-pearl blotting book, and all silver laid on table. Left behind plated ware, fire irons, chimney-glasses, rosewood cottage piano.

**Fifine's Later Life (Chapter 23)**: Subsequently kept milliner's shop in Rue du Helder, Paris, as Madame de Saint-Amaranthe, living "with great credit" under Steyne's patronage. Spoke of England "as of the most treacherous country in the world."

**Household Mutiny (Chapter 23)**: Cook with blackened face seated on chintz sofa beside Mrs. Raggles, administering Maraschino, defiantly declaring wages unpaid; page putting fingers in cream dish; footman talking to Raggles (face full of perplexity and woe); servants entirely indifferent to Rebecca's calls. Footman Trotter, drunk and inebriated, accused: "He ain't a coming back...You're no better than swindlers, both on you." Servants demanded unpaid wages.

**Raggles's Lament (Chapter 23)**: Raggles wept: "I never thought to live to see this year day: I've known the Crawley family ever since I was born...one of that family was a goin' to ruing me." Owed milk and butter bill of two hundred pounds. Bills coming due next week with no means to meet them. Would be sold up and turned out of shop and house.

## Rebecca's Final Attempt at Reconciliation (Chapter 23)

**Rebecca's Audacious Lie (Chapter 23)**: When servants demanded payment, Rebecca claimed: "Colonel Crawley had settled with you. He will to-morrow. I declare to you upon my honour that he left home this morning with fifteen hundred pounds in his pocket-book." **CRITICAL LIE**: Rawdon actually left with considerably less. Promised payment from appointment with "good appointment."

**Rebecca's Appeal to Pitt (Chapter 23)**: At four o'clock walked swiftly down streets (no money for carriage) to Sir Pitt's door in Great Gaunt Street. Lady Jane at church. Slipped past sentinel in livery into Sir Pitt's study. Told Sir Pitt: "It is true. Lord Steyne told me on Friday night...Mr. Martyr, the Colonial Secretary, told him yesterday that it was made out." **CLAIM (UNVERIFIED)**: Rawdon promised appointment by Colonial Secretary. Rebecca poured false story into ears of perplexed kinsman, insisting she was guilty only of devotedness and had received Steyne alone a hundred times before.

**Lady Jane's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: Lady Jane entered trembling and pale, having sent maid after breakfast to learn full story from Raggles. Said: "I am surprised that woman has the audacity to enter this house." Made ultimatum: "I declare that I will not bear that--that woman again under my roof; if she enters it, I and my children will leave it. You--you must choose, sir, between her and me." Sir Pitt attempted interruption but Lady Jane swept out, fluttering with her own audacity.

**Rebecca's Success with Pitt (Chapter 23)**: Becky was not hurt; was pleased. "It was the diamond-clasp you gave me," she said to Sir Pitt. Before she left him, Baronet had promised to seek out his brother and endeavour to bring about reconciliation.

## The Governorship Announcement and Wenham's Intervention (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1392–1399)

**Governorship Announcement (Excerpt 1393)**: Newspaper announcement appeared: "GOVERNORSHIP OF COVENTRY ISLAND.--H.M.S. Yellowjack, Commander Jaunders, has brought letters and papers from Coventry Island. H. E. Sir Thomas Liverseege had fallen a victim to the prevailing fever at Swampton...We hear that the Governorship has been offered to Colonel Rawdon Crawley, C.B., a distinguished Waterloo officer...the gentleman selected by the Colonial Office to fill the lamented vacancy...is admirably calculated for the post which he is about to occupy." **Three thousand a year, delightful climate, excellent government-house, certain promotion.**

**At the Regent Club (Excerpt 1392–1394)**: Rawdon at Club reading newspaper when man said, "Crawley, I congratulate you." Macmurdo laughed: "You must take me out as your secretary, old boy." As Crawley and Macmurdo sat wondering and perplexed, Club waiter brought card of Mr. Wenham, who begged to see Colonel Crawley. Wenham greeted Macmurdo cordially; Macmurdo put out one finger armed with buckskin glove and made frigid bow over tight cravat, discontented at being put in communication with inferior when Lord Steyne should have sent Colonel.

**Wenham's Arguments (Excerpts 1396–1399)**: Wenham attempted to convince Rawdon he was in wrong, using parliamentary oratory: "Look at the matter as a man of the world--as an honest man--and see if you have not been in the wrong. You come home from a journey, and find--what?--my Lord Steyne supping at your house in Curzon Street with Mrs. Crawley. Is the circumstance strange or novel? Has he not been a hundred times before in the same position?" Declared Rebecca innocent: "I believe that Mrs. Crawley is as innocent as my wife, Mrs. Wenham." Claimed Rawdon's suspicions "monstrous and utterly unfounded" and injured "an honourable gentleman who has proved his good-will towards you by a thousand benefactions--and a most spotless and innocent lady."

**Wenham's Account of Steyne's Condition (Excerpt 1397)**: Wenham reported being "sent for this morning by my Lord Steyne, and found him in a pitiable state, as, I need hardly inform Colonel Crawley, any man of age and infirmity would be after a personal conflict with a man of your strength...It was a cruel advantage you took of that strength, Colonel Crawley...A man whom he had loaded with benefits and regarded with affection had subjected him to the foulest indignity. What was this very appointment, which appears in the journals of to-day, but a proof of his kindness to you?"

**Wenham's Peace Initiative (Excerpt 1398–1399)**: Wenham claimed he sat by Steyne's bedside "for an hour or more...beseeching, imploring Lord Steyne to forego his intention of demanding a meeting." Argued duel would create public scandal. Claimed circumstantial suspicions were understandable but that madness of jealousy should not lead to duel. **Alleged (PLAN)**: Wenham reported having implored Steyne not to send the challenge, but text indicates Steyne did send challenge; Wenham now attempting to convince Rawdon to decline meeting.

## Key Relationships and Character States

**Rawdon**: Complete moral regeneration. Prepared for death; entrusted son to Pitt and Jane; settled debts; arranged duel as matter of honor. Discovered Coventry Island Governorship offered (three thousand a year). Currently at Regent Club with Macmurdo receiving Wenham's arguments against duel. Maintains honor despite Wenham's attempt to convince him he was wrong.

**Rebecca**: Utterly ruined yet resourceful. Exposed as Steyne's paid mistress. Household collapsed—landlord in possession, servants drunk and mutinous, maid fled with plunder. Spreading false claims: Rawdon left with fifteen hundred pounds (lie); promised appointment (unverified). Successfully manipulated Pitt into promise of reconciliation despite Lady Jane's ultimatum.

**Steyne**: Scarred by assault; remaining in position of power through Wenham. Sent challenge (subsequently); now attempting to dissuade Rawdon through Wenham's intervention. Supporting Fifine in Paris.

**Pitt and Lady Jane**: Jane rescued Rawdon from spunging-house; entrusted with little Rawdon's guardianship. Pitt promised six hundred pounds for Briggs and little Rawdon. Pitt promised to seek reconciliation at Rebecca's urging. Lady Jane made ultimatum choosing between Rebecca and her family.

**Captain Macmurdo**: Conducting duel arrangements professionally. Now present at Regent Club where Wenham attempts to mediate.

**Mr. Wenham**: Parliamentary orator; Steyne's emissary. Attempting to convince Rawdon his suspicions unfounded; that Rebecca innocent; that duel would disgrace all parties; that Steyne magnanimous and kind; that he (Wenham) has implored Steyne not to send challenge. **Factual status of claims**: Wenham's portrayal of events contradicts earlier narrative; appears designed to discourage duel through appeals to honor and reputation.

**CRITICAL STATE**: Duel formally initiated. Wenham now intervening at Regent Club to dissuade Rawdon from accepting/proceeding with meeting. Governorship announcement appeared in press, confirming Steyne's (apparent) patronage gift. Rawdon's immediate prospects transformed by appointment; yet duel remains imminent. Pitt promised reconciliation; Lady Jane threatened departure if Rebecca enters house again. Rebecca's household completely dissolved; her future uncertain.
